title: The filesystem is one tree
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read any Linux path and say where it points, and you know what lives in the directories you will meet most often.

blocks.text: Windows gives you several trees: C:, D:, a network drive. Linux gives you exactly one. It starts at / — called root — and everything on the machine hangs somewhere beneath it, including extra disks and USB sticks, which get attached at a folder rather than getting a letter of their own.

blocks.title: One tree, one consequence
blocks.text: Because there is only one tree, every file on the machine has exactly one full address. That is what makes Linux scriptable: a path in a script means the same thing on every machine of that type.
The directories worth knowing on day one

rows: Where you work. Usually written as ~
Almost every server setting you change is here
Where you go when something went wrong
Where the commands you type actually live
Writable by everyone — which makes it interesting to attackers

blocks.title: "Everything is a file"
blocks.text: You will hear this constantly. It means Linux exposes hardware, running processes, and system state as things you can read with ordinary file commands. A disk, a network connection, even a running process shows up somewhere in the tree. It sounds like trivia; it is why one small set of commands can inspect the entire system.

An absolute path starts at / and is unambiguous from anywhere: /var/log/syslog means one specific file, no matter where you are standing. A relative path starts from wherever you currently are: log/syslog means "the log folder here", which depends entirely on your current location.

items: / at the start means absolute — measured from the root of the tree
no leading / means relative — measured from where you are now

blocks.title: Where this bites people
blocks.text: A script that uses relative paths does the right thing when you run it from your own folder and something else entirely when a scheduled job runs it from elsewhere. When a task works by hand and fails on a schedule, relative paths are the first suspect.

blocks.title: Read the tree yourself
steps: Run: ls /etc | head  (see the first few config files)
Run: echo ~          (see what ~ expands to for you)
blocks.expected: A list of the standard top-level folders, a sample of configuration files, and your own home path — probably /home/ plus your username.

cheatsheet: Linux has one tree starting at / — no drive letters
/usr/bin = installed programs · /tmp = world-writable scratch · /root = root's home
Absolute path starts with / and means the same from anywhere
Relative path depends on where you are: . here, .. up one, ~ home
Task works by hand but fails on a schedule? Suspect relative paths

checkpoint.prompt: What is the difference between /log and log ?

choices.A: No difference, the slash is optional
choices.B: /log is absolute — a folder directly under the root of the tree. log is relative — a folder inside wherever you currently are
choices.C: /log is a file and log is a folder

checkpoint.explanation: The leading slash anchors the path to the root of the single tree. Without it, the path is measured from your current directory.

checkpoint.prompt: Where would you look first for configuration of a service on a Linux server?
checkpoint.explanation: /etc holds system configuration as plain text. /var/log holds output about what happened, /usr/bin holds the programs, and /tmp is scratch space.

checkpoint.prompt: A scheduled job runs a script that works perfectly when you run it by hand. What is worth checking first?

choices.A: Whether the script uses relative paths that resolve differently depending on the working directory
choices.C: Whether the file has a .sh extension
choices.D: Whether the machine has been restarted

checkpoint.explanation: A relative path silently means something different when the working directory changes. It is the classic cause of "works for me, fails on schedule".
